questions.prompt: Which particulate description best represents a typical ionic crystal?
options: An extended periodic three-dimensional arrangement balancing unlike-ion attractions and like-ion repulsions.
Separate neutral molecules held only by weak intermolecular attractions
All cations clustered on one side and all anions on the other
Only neutral atoms sharing a common pool of delocalized electrons
questions.explanation: A is correct. The lattice organizes charged particles to lower net electrostatic energy without treating the solid as isolated neutral molecules. B is incorrect: that describes a molecular solid rather than the ionic lattice model. C is incorrect: charge separation and like-charge crowding are unfavorable. D is incorrect: that is a metallic model, not an ionic crystal.

questions.prompt: A particulate model of MgCl2(s) represents complete neutral bulk composition. Which ion-count ratio is required?
options: One Mg2+ for every one Cl−
Two Mg2+ for every one Cl−
One Mg2+ for every two Cl−.
Equal numbers of Mg atoms and neutral Cl2 molecules
questions.explanation: C is correct. A+2 cation requires two−1 anions for net neutrality, matching the formula-unit ratio. A is incorrect: that gives net+1 charge per pair. B is incorrect: that gives net+3 charge per group. D is incorrect: the model must represent the ions in the stated ionic solid.

questions.prompt: A crystal contains M2+ cations and X3− anions. What smallest whole-number formula ratio gives a neutral solid?
options: M2X3
MX
M3X
M3X2
questions.explanation: D is correct. Three+2 ions and two−3 ions give+6−6=0. A is incorrect: that gives+4−9, not zero. B is incorrect: that gives net−1 per pair. C is incorrect: that gives net+3 per group.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a one-to-one M+/X− crystal correctly relates nearest-neighbor arrangement to electrostatic attraction?
options: Every ion should have only neighbors of the same charge
A stable local arrangement generally places opposite charges near one another rather than grouping like charges together.
Cations attract cations because both have lost electrons
Opposite charges should be separated as far as possible to maximize attraction
questions.explanation: B is correct. Unlike-charge attraction favors neighboring opposite ions, with the complete lattice also accounting for other repulsions and attractions. A is incorrect: that emphasizes repulsion. C is incorrect: like charges repel. D is incorrect: attraction weakens with separation.

questions.prompt: Why can shifting planes in an ionic crystal cause brittle fracture?
options: Ions become neutral atoms whenever a plane moves
Every ionic solid has mobile metallic electrons that lubricate the planes
The shift can bring like-charged ions into adjacent positions, creating strong repulsion.
Oppositely charged ions begin to repel solely because the solid is strained
questions.explanation: C is correct. A displacement can disrupt the favorable alternating-charge arrangement and separate the lattice. A is incorrect: mechanical displacement does not automatically transfer electrons to neutralize ions. B is incorrect: that is not the ionic-lattice model. D is incorrect: their charge signs still produce attraction; unfavorable like-charge alignments matter.

questions.prompt: Why is a typical ionic crystal a poor electrical conductor while its melt can conduct?
options: In the crystal the ions are constrained in lattice positions; in the melt they can move and carry charge.
The crystal contains no charged particles
Melting must convert every ion into a free electron
The melt conducts because its ions become stationary
questions.explanation: A is correct. The carriers are already charged in both states, but their mobility changes. B is incorrect: the lattice consists of ions. C is incorrect: mobile ions, not that conversion, explain molten conduction. D is incorrect: charge transport requires mobility.

questions.prompt: A drawing depicts NaCl(s) as widely separated, independent NaCl molecules. What key feature is missing from this ionic-solid model?
options: An obligatory two-atom covalent molecule for every formula unit
The extended network of electrostatic interactions among many neighboring ions.
A requirement that all ions have zero charge
A specific memorized coordination number for every possible ionic solid
questions.explanation: B is correct. A formula unit gives a composition ratio, not a boundary around an isolated molecule in the lattice. A is incorrect: that retains the mistaken molecular interpretation. C is incorrect: removing ionic charges would discard the defining interactions. D is incorrect: the general lattice model does not require memorizing a particular crystal structure.

questions.prompt: A model labels every nearest separation in an ionic solid as attractive and includes no repulsive interactions anywhere. Why is this incomplete?
options: Every unlike-charge interaction must instead be repulsive
No electrostatic interaction occurs in a neutral solid
Repulsion matters only in gases, never solids
Like-charge ions and short-range overlap also contribute repulsion to the lattice energy balance.
questions.explanation: D is correct. A stable arrangement reflects competing interactions rather than attraction without limit. A is incorrect: opposite ionic charges attract. B is incorrect: bulk neutrality does not eliminate local charged-particle interactions. C is incorrect: repulsions are important in condensed structures too.

questions.prompt: A simplified NaCl model is given the ionic-size information that Na+ is smaller than Cl−. Which representation is consistent with that information and bulk neutrality?
options: Twice as many smaller+1 spheres as larger−1 spheres
Equal numbers of smaller+1 spheres and larger−1 spheres in an extended arrangement.
Equal numbers with the+1 spheres drawn larger despite the supplied sizes
Only one type of uncharged sphere
questions.explanation: B is correct. The supplied size ordering and1:1 charge balance must both be represented. A is incorrect: that gives excess positive charge. C is incorrect: that contradicts the stated ionic-radius relationship. D is incorrect: that omits both ion identities and electrostatic structure.

questions.prompt: A complete neutral bulk model of an M+/X− ionic solid is enlarged without changing its composition. What must happen to the particle-count ratio?
options: The cation fraction must increase with crystal size
The formula subscripts must equal the total numbers in each larger sample
It stays1:1 even though the total number of represented ions increases.
The larger model must contain neutral molecules instead of ions
questions.explanation: C is correct. Extending a crystal adds proportional numbers of cations and anions; it does not change its formula ratio. A is incorrect: bulk neutrality and composition constrain the ratio. B is incorrect: formula units express reduced composition, not sample size. D is incorrect: sample size does not change bonding type.

questions.prompt: An ionic lattice model uses the same charges but allows opposite-ion centers to collapse to zero separation, claiming unlimited stability. Which correction is essential?
options: Include short-range repulsion and finite ion size, which prevent unbounded collapse.
Remove all attraction between opposite charges
Assume ions have no electrons and no finite extent
Treat point-charge attraction as accurate at every separation without any overlap correction
questions.explanation: A is correct. Real stable separations result from a balance; a point-charge attraction alone is incomplete at extremely short range. B is incorrect: attraction is real and remains part of the model. C is incorrect: that removes the physical origin of important short-range effects. D is incorrect: the point-charge-only approximation omits the short-range physics that prevents collapse.
